verified.label: Verified
verified.note: Read directly from an artifact — a constant in a disassembly, a literal in a script, a symbol in a table, a part number in a service manual. Not dependent on interpretation.

inferred.label: Inferred
inferred.note: A reading of verified evidence that is well supported but not directly stated. The reasoning is given, and so are the competing readings.

unknown.label: Unknown
unknown.note: The artifacts show it exists, but its content, layout or semantics have not been determined.

public.label: Public
public.note: Taken from a datasheet, standard, service manual or the manufacturer's own published documentation. No analysis was needed.

platforms.summary: A nine-processor console whose mixing DSPs have no instruction memory at all — the audio path is fixed-function silicon configured through a register file.
platforms.headline: The five YSS919C "DSP7" mixing chips expose a 512-word register file and no program port. This was proven not just from the pin tables but from absence: every region of the 64 MB flash is accounted for and there is no DSP7 program image anywhere in it.
platforms.method: Static analysis of the V5.91 USB firmware update package, cross-referenced against the published service manual's LSI pin descriptions. No console was involved and no hardware was inspected.

`QL-MD103.BIN` — 110 KB channel-name display sub-MCU image
`FWUpdate_QL1_v4020401_sw310.dnt` — 4.7 MB Audinate Brooklyn II package
Service manual, LSI PIN DESCRIPTION section
`QL Editor.app` — Premium Rack plugins shipped as unstripped x86_64 dylibs

programmable.note: The cheapest route to putting custom DSP in the audio path with no console modification at all. Host aperture 0xBA002000 + (slot << 11), 16-bit port on A10..A1.
The audio crossbar between Dante, every DSP7, the SHARC, the DSP6 bank and both slots. JTAG header present, and it is configurable from the CPU. Highest leverage, least investigated.

The Premium Rack engine. A documented part, SPI-slave boot, JTAG header already fitted. Eight stereo slots means up to 16 mono inserts, patchable from the console's own UI. The one place third-party code could plausibly run.

platforms.verdict: The mixing engine is closed by construction rather than by policy — there is no software on it to replace. The programmable surface is real but sits alongside the mix engine, not inside it.
openQuestions: The patch FPGA's configuration path from the CPU has not been traced.
The DSP7 register-file semantics are undocumented; only the bus interface is known.
No claim here has been checked against a physical QL console.
traps: The image load base is 0x8803BF80, not 0x88000000. The wrong value looks entirely plausible and silently yields almost no valid cross-references.
Never attribute an MMIO constant from string-pool proximity. Doing so produced a claim that 0xBA002000 was the DSP7 window when it is the slot aperture — published, then retracted.

platforms.summary: Nine years newer than the QL and sharing almost nothing with it but the parameter framework — including, crucially, the same DSP philosophy.
platforms.headline: The update package is a named-component archive (`#YAMAHA MBDFArchive`) carrying a full Linux rootfs, and the installer is a plain bash script with no checksum ceremony and no signature. Unlike the QL, the DSP arrives as a loadable 3.8 MB image.
platforms.method: Static analysis of the V3.00 firmware package (167 MB) and the macOS DM3 Editor. Nothing has been tested on hardware.
artifacts: `DM3_firmware_V3.00.bin` — 167 MB, eleven named components
`DM3 Editor.app` (macOS)

hardware.value: Runs a Linux userland — component 1 is an 88 MB rootfs tarball

hardware.label: FPGA
hardware.value: Present — component 3, `fab_V110.bin`, 539 KB inflated

hardware.label: DSP
hardware.value: Present as a loadable image — component 4, `DSP_V121.bin`, 3.80 MB inflated

software.label: Container format
software.value: `#YAMAHA MBDFArchive` — magic, model, version and a 16-byte digest, then `#FIRMWARE` records of five BE u32 fields, three NUL-terminated strings (path / description / version) and a zlib payload, terminated by `#END`

software.label: Main application
software.value: `app_console.tgz`, 64.8 MB inflated, V3.00

software.label: Installer
software.value: A bash script. Untars to /tmp/update, walks /yamaha/firmware.new/, compares each component's version file against the installed one and copies only what changed, running a per-component `<name>.sh` hook if present

software.label: Bootloader
software.value: Shipped as an updatable component — `app_bootloader.tgz`, V1.03

security.value: None — the installer performs no signature check

security.label: Integrity
security.value: A 16-byte digest in the archive header; no checksum ceremony in the install path

security.label: Encryption
security.value: None — every component is zlib, and unpacks with a 60-line script

programmable.note: A conventional userland behind an unsigned, script-driven installer is a materially different proposition from the QL's µITRON image.
Unlike the QL's fixed-function DSP7s, the DM3 loads a 3.8 MB DSP image at update time. What accepts it has not been identified.

platforms.verdict: The interesting contrast with the QL is not the CPU or the OS — it is that the DSP is loadable here. That single fact changes what a modification would even mean on this platform.
openQuestions: Which silicon consumes `DSP_V121.bin`, and in what format.
The FPGA part has not been identified.
No board has been inspected and no claim has been checked on hardware.

platforms.summary: A 55 MB firmware image that contains none of the mixer. The entire audio path lives in FPGA fabric behind an undocumented AXI register map.
platforms.headline: The update package is 55 MB of ARM image and 2.5 MB of bitstream — and the 2.5 MB is the mixer. Most of the 55 MB is uncompressed UI artwork.
platforms.method: Static analysis of a single vendor firmware update file. No hardware was inspected. The firmware image was not retained, so the analysis currently cannot be re-derived without obtaining it again.
artifacts: `SQ-5UPG_1_6_3r6268.bin` — three records, no compression, no encryption

hardware.label: SoC
hardware.value: Xilinx Zynq-7000 XC7Z020 — proven from the bitstream's IDCODE configuration packet (30018001 → 03727093), not inferred

hardware.label: Corroboration
hardware.value: Linked Xilinx PS drivers: xemacps, xscugic, xdevcfg, xqspips, xiicps, xttcps, xuartps, plus lwIP 2.0.3 (xilinx_modified)

hardware.label: FPGA count
hardware.value: One. xdevcfg with PCAP_FPGA_DONE_FAIL shows the bitstream loading into this same chip's PL over the PCAP bridge — there is no second FPGA

hardware.label: DRAM
hardware.value: ≥1 GB — inferred from CPU1's 0x20100000 load address (513 MB in) against the Zynq-7000 PS ceiling of 1 GB. No memory-controller config was decoded

hardware.label: Boot flash
hardware.value: Dual-parallel QSPI NOR, ~64 MB (`InitQspi2Dual`). Dual-parallel means two devices striped — a naive single-chip dump gets every other byte

hardware.label: Surface MCU
hardware.value: A fader/surface MCU flashed over SPI from the ARM (`Expected Fader Version %u.%u, updating...`)

hardware.label: FX board
hardware.value: Separate board with its own DSPs and SDRAM (`FX board ID 0x%02X not recognised`, `FX[0] failed SDRAM test`)

software.label: Operating system
software.value: None. Zero FreeRTOS, ThreadX or Linux strings — a bare-metal Xilinx standalone BSP with a custom message-block system and a custom GUI

software.label: Core model
software.value: AMP across both Cortex-A9s, not SMP. `CPU0: sending Start Msg to CPU1`

software.label: CPU0
software.value: `sQu_Host` at 0x00100000 — mixer control, GUI, protocols

software.label: CPU1
software.value: `sQu_USB` at 0x20100000 — SQ-Drive: USB host, FAT, WAV. Directory layout /AHSQ/USBRec, /AHSQ/Scenes, /AHSQ/Shows appears verbatim

software.label: Container header
software.value: 0x70 (112) bytes, computed as next_offset − this_offset − payload_len and confirmed independently at both gaps. It is not read from any field

software.label: Payload format
software.value: Despite `.elf` names the payloads are raw ARM32 images, each with a 16-byte preamble; byte 16 onward is the ARM exception vector table

software.label: Code fraction
software.value: Only ~10–16 MB of the 55 MB host image is code. From 16 MB on it compresses to 9–27%, i.e. uncompressed artwork and fonts

security.label: Image signing
security.value: None. No RSA, SHA or AES strings anywhere in either image

security.label: Update validation
security.value: CRC only — `VerifyFlash Expected CRC to be 0x%lx, but calculated 0x%lx`

security.label: Bitstream encryption
security.value: Not encrypted. The CTL0 write is 0x00001501 with the DEC bit (bit 6) clear and no key-load sequence, so the bitstream is analysable

security.label: Recovery
security.value: A/B image banks with Zynq multiboot. The update overwrites the inactive bank; the first-stage bootloader is not in the update file and is not protected by the A/B scheme

security.label: Entitlement
security.value: An entitlement mechanism exists and was identified. Analysis stopped there — see the methodology page

programmable.note: The SLink slot takes gigaACE, Dante and Waves cards, and Allen & Heath publish the SQ MIDI/TCP control protocol. This is where the value is.
Unencrypted, and Project X-Ray covers Artix-7 and Zynq-7 fabric. But replacing it means writing a 48-channel 96 kHz engine against an unpublished pinout.
Replaceable, and the Zynq is maximally Linux-friendly. It also gets you Linux wired to a black box, because none of the mixer is in the software you would be replacing.

platforms.verdict: A poor rehosting target, but not for the usual reasons. There is no secure boot and no signing — yet none of the mixer is in the software you would replace. If it were ever pursued, the correct first move is JTAG, not the USB update path: dump the 64 MB QSPI intact before writing anything.
openQuestions: The PL's AXI register map is entirely undocumented — this is the whole audio path.
The first-stage bootloader is not in the update file and has never been seen.
The debug UART is near-certainly populated (xuartps is linked and printf diagnostics are everywhere) but has never been located on a board.
traps: A parser assuming a 0x24 or 0x40 container header parses record 0 plausibly and then lands mid-payload in 55 MB of ARM code and artwork.
The correct load mapping for the host image is VA = file offset + 0x103DD0, pinned empirically from the GUI string-pointer table — not the 0x100000 the container header implies.
GUI strings are reached through a master string-pointer table indexed by string ID, so they have no direct LDR-literal cross-reference. Only BSP and system strings are loaded directly.

platforms.summary: The only platform here being studied to build on rather than to understand — and the only one where the container format was analysed, found opaque, and then declared off the critical path.
platforms.headline: The `.wingfw` container is opaque but structured, and specifically not a block cipher: index of coincidence is flat at 3.06 across every stride from 1 to 1024, and all 171 constant runs of ≥64 bytes are 0xFF with zero 0x00 runs. No block cipher leaves those.
platforms.method: Static analysis of a vendor firmware image, plus published datasheets and standards. No hardware has been acquired, so every hardware row is provisional and marked accordingly. A written clean-room policy governs the project.
artifacts: A `.wingfw` release image, version 3.1.1 (fullsize variant — nothing learned from it may be assumed to hold for Compact)
NXP i.MX 6 datasheet and reference manual
Analog Devices and Efinix product documentation

Documented parts. Bringing them up from nothing, alongside the Trion bitstream and AES50, is the mountain.

programmable.item: USB audio on the host port
programmable.note: The measurement path that can never be blocked by the FPGA and DSP work — deliberately staged first for exactly that reason.

platforms.verdict: Hardware-wise the most open platform surveyed, and the only one where a full replacement OS is a coherent goal. Everything now rests on two cheap lid-off questions and one fuse.
openQuestions: Is the i.MX 6 serial-download path reachable, and are the HAB fuses unburned? Everything else is downstream of this.
Discrete PHY behind each etherCON, or straight to fabric?
Is anything in the clock tree steerable?
traps: A 3-byte magic such as gzip's appears about 2.3 times by chance in 38 MB, and scanning 514 transforms means scanning 263 MB — expect roughly 16 coincidental hits. An early verdict called the firmware "a known container" on exactly that basis.
Every negative sweep result needs a positive control. A broken sweep and a genuine absence look identical.

platforms.summary: Not a console, but the transport a great many of them hang off. Documented from both ends at once — the server firmware and the host driver are the same protocol version.
platforms.headline: The SoundGrid Server is a hard-realtime appliance, not a general-purpose Linux box. Its kernel command line isolates every worker core from the scheduler, RCU, tick, idle and frequency scaling, and SoundGrid frames are steered to a dedicated uncoalesced hardware receive queue.
platforms.method: Static analysis of vendor-distributed binaries and configuration files already present on a machine holding a licensed installation. No Waves source code, NDA material or SDK was involved. Techniques: reading plain-text scripts, demangling C++ symbol and RTTI tables, extracting strings, and disassembling a small number of functions in the GPL kernel module.
artifacts: SoundGrid Driver (macOS kext) 16.5.15.119 — unstripped C++ symbols
SGS firmware image `SGS_16.5`, External_Version 16.5.79.183 — extracted SquashFS
`AG_NSServer` — stripped ELF, retains C++ RTTI
`wsgnf.ko` — GPL-licensed kernel module, unstripped
141 × `.wfi` per-model I/O firmware files, referenced by name only

hardware.label: Server platform
hardware.value: x86_64 appliance; the binary names an Intel I225-V 2.5GbE-class controller

hardware.label: Boot
hardware.value: SYSLINUX/EFI into a RAM-resident root filesystem — SquashFS (zstd) initrd on /dev/ram0, overlaid read-write on tmpfs and pivot_root'ed into

hardware.label: Base distribution
hardware.value: ryolinux-release 4.3, Buildroot-derived, hostname `buildroot`

hardware.label: Kernel
hardware.value: 6.12.11 SMP PREEMPT_RT — fully preemptible realtime

hardware.label: Link layer
hardware.value: EtherType 0x8908, steered by ethtool receive-flow rules to hardware queue 1 with interrupt coalescing disabled (rx-frames 1, tx-frames 1)

software.label: Process model
software.value: A single userland process, `AG_NSServer` (AudioGrid Network Shell Server), owns the protocol. It starts before the network stack is brought up

software.label: Realtime partitioning
software.value: Command-line options name a control core, a master core and a worker core set, plus AudioGrid and kernel CPU reserve percentages

software.label: Kernel fast path
software.value: `wsgnf.ko` — character device, an mmap region shared with userland, ioctls for sample-set enable/disable and interface naming, and /proc debug and stats entries

software.label: Shared mapping
software.value: Carries at least a mutex and a switch timestamp — the latter being how userland and kernel agree on the exact sample instant a configuration change takes effect

software.label: Protocol shape
software.value: Not a flat command set. A set of node families, each with its own protocol version, addressed by node number, each exposing a description-get operation plus family-specific commands

software.label: Self-description
software.value: The server can emit its own protocol description as XML (`-M`, node protocol xml). Capturing that output is the single highest-value next step

security.label: Scope boundary
security.value: Licensing, authorisation and entitlement mechanisms are explicitly out of scope and were not analysed

security.label: GPL obligation
security.value: `wsgnf.ko` declares license=GPL in its module metadata and is distributed in binary form as part of a product. The source-availability obligation applies on its own terms. No claim is made here about whether it has been met

programmable.note: The stated goal: a device that appears on a SoundGrid network as a discoverable node, recovers the network sample clock, and exchanges multichannel audio with servers and I/O devices.

platforms.verdict: The most conventionally documentable platform here, because both sides of the same protocol version were available and corroborate each other — the driver names its C++ classes and the server names its message types.
openQuestions: No claim has been validated against live hardware. Nothing has been tested against a real SoundGrid network.
Every wire layout should be treated as provisional until a packet capture confirms it.
The XML self-description has not yet been captured from a running server.
traps: This is not black-box analysis and should never be described as such — the findings come substantially from inspecting vendor binaries.
It is not clean-room analysis either, because no implementation exists yet and therefore no team separation has been established. Both terms are commonly misapplied to work of this kind.

platforms.summary: Control-plane work rather than a firmware teardown — undertaken to drive the console from a bespoke surface rather than to understand its internals.
platforms.headline: The console's own VSKP protocol over TCP 1703 was mapped and then deliberately relegated to a fallback, because layer state, channel selection and sends-on-fader live only inside the control application and are not console parameters at all.
platforms.method: Behavioural analysis against Mixing Station 3.1.2 running offline as a dMix 128. Offline mode models the full 213-channel data tree, so parameter facts are solid; anything requiring a physical MIDI device or the real console is untested. No console, control surface or panel hardware exists.
artifacts: Mixing Station 3.1.2 desktop, offline dMix 128 profile
Generated parameter map — regenerated by script, not hand-edited

No physical MIDI device has been exercised against the mapping.
traps: A surface that talks straight to the console cannot know which layer is up or which channel is selected — those are application state, not console state.

platforms.summary: Not a teardown. The open console these teardowns keep pointing at — included because "what would you build instead" is the question every one of them ends on.
platforms.headline: 128 inputs, 64 buses, every channel strip computed in FPGA fabric at 96 kHz, speaking Dante, RAVENNA/AES67 and AVB/Milan simultaneously. Where the commercial platforms hide the mixer behind an undocumented register map, here the register map is the deliverable.
platforms.method: Original design work. Correctness rests on a bit-accurate fixed-point model in Rust, replayed against the RTL in Verilator.
